content: The Mediterranean diet is a dietary pattern traditionally followed by people living in countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea. It emphasizes consumption of plant-based foods, such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds; olive oil as the main source of fat; moderate amounts of fish and poultry; limited red meat; and a moderate intake of dairy products and red wine. This diet is linked to several mechanisms that promote health, including anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, improved lipid profiles, better blood sugar regulation, and favorable impacts on blood pressure and vascular function. Extensive epidemiological and clinical research demonstrates that adherence to the Mediterranean diet reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases, certain cancers, and metabolic disorders. Its practical relevance lies in its palatability, flexibility, and inclusion of diverse nutrient-rich foods, making it an accessible and sustainable option for many adults. However, limitations include that the diet can vary regionally, and some formulations may be higher in calories if not balanced well; cost and availability of some components may also be barriers. Important related concepts include the role of dietary fat quality, the benefits of whole versus refined grains, and cultural adaptations of the diet. Overall, the Mediterranean diet is considered a model of healthy eating with robust evidence supporting cardiovascular and metabolic health benefits.
